en: The first reflection, "The Crushing of Arrogance," is for the sake of pacifying all obstacles, because it causes the serpent of arrogance to slither away.
To the one who is the treasury of truth and nectar, and who expands as self-luminous light.
Homage again and again to solitude, which leads away from cyclic existence, which removes the arrogance of the mind, and which is a sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility.
(These two together:
Kṣemendra, out of affection for his friends and as a physician for the disease of pride,
exerts himself for their well-being with the sweet medicines of well-spoken verses.
Lineage, wealth, learning, beauty, heroism, generosity, and likewise asceticism—
these seven are primarily the causes of pride among human beings.
For the benefit of embodied beings who are overwhelmed by egoism— just as one might act for the sake of living creatures— I compose this "Crushing of Pride" to pacify delusion.

For those who, out of delusion, falsely pride themselves on their lineage by claiming "this is our family, that is our family," we do not know what kind of stiff-necked planetary seizure has taken hold of them.
If one searches for the root of a family, which is like a lotus, once it has been submerged in the mud of faults, then it will inevitably become exposed.
Just as it is impossible for a noble thoroughbred horse to be called anything other than noble,
so too a son born into that same lineage cannot be devoid of virtue if his father possesses virtue.
If one man in the family is a performer of sacrifices, deeply learned, and a man of former virtue,
while another is a doer of evil and a fool— to which of these two would the family conform?
In this world, a lineage persists only so long as there is a continuity of past tradition;
once the power of its virtues is severed, the entire lineage comes to an end.
What pride of lineage can there be for those born in a lowly station, whose mothers are like rivers that erode the very banks of their family? (KDarp 1.11)
For one who is truly of noble birth, what is the use of that lineage when, out of shame for newfound poverty, he must utter the wretched pleas of a beggar before those of low birth?
Even if born into a family of virtuous qualities, by whom is one devoid of virtue honored?
To whom is a cow useful that, though born from a lineage of milch cows, is barren?
Therefore, since you yourself are the founder of your lineage, reflect upon this and abandon your pride;
knowing that family depends upon virtues, let your mind be devoted to virtues.

When one constantly reflects upon the search for their origins, there is no lineage of men where women alone extend the succession of the thread of progeny. Who truly knows the secret conduct rooted in passion that has become entwined before these women, who appear so modest in their fabricated displays of artifice?
If the mother, grandmother, or great-grandmother of one who is adorned by family pride is corrupted by the inherent nature of women, then this fault strikes at the very root of the lineage.
In the solar dynasty, there was the king Triśaṅku who became an outcaste;
likewise, Dilīpa, Raghu, Rāma, and others were monarchs born of that same lineage.
Among the kings of the Lunar dynasty, he who was the ancestor, Budha,
became world-renowned for having violated his teacher’s bed with the wife of Candra.
Karna is the son of Kanyā, and the sons of Pāṇḍu are born of the wife;
what further need is there for other discourses on common lineages?

Formerly, in Mathurā, there lived a Brāhmaṇa who was the best among the illustrious; he was a performer of sacrifices named Śrutanidhi, possessed of Vedic learning and renowned for his mastery of the scriptures.
He had a beloved wife named Muktālatā, born of a noble lineage, whose form was charming with loveliness.
To her was born a beloved son named Tejonidhi, who was of excellent conduct, the foremost among the virtuous, and a stainless mirror for knowledge.
That wise man, a scholar learned in the Vedas, a poet, and a repository of all the arts,
caused the heads of the learned men in the assemblies to bow down in shame.
To soothe him, who was feverish with the affliction of pride and afflicted by a stiff neck, his father affectionately began to speak words of salutary advice in private.
O son, why have you fallen into such folly through false pride,
that mounted upon an elephant of intoxication, you feel shame before those worthy of honor?
There is no means in this cycle of existence for those fools who fall into the pit of pride, by which a momentary handhold could be provided to them.
Alas! By whom was this pride, which is shunned by virtuous people and arises from family, learning, and wealth, taught to you, whose memory of discipline has been destroyed? (KDarp 1.27)
Family ties are unstable; learning is always subject to dispute;
pride leads only to delusion; and wealth perishes in an instant, being utterly false.
This alone is true nobility, this alone is the acquisition of virtue:
that the heads of the virtuous are always bowed in humility before those who are even more virtuous.
Compassion alone is recognized as true knowledge; truth alone is imperishable wealth;
for those possessing stainless discernment, virtuous conduct alone is a pure lineage.
For those of lofty mind, prosperity is blessed with enjoyment, their lineage is brightened by freedom from wretchedness, and their learning is clear through the absence of pride. (KDarp 1.31)
For whom is hatred not a source of fault? For whom is affection not for their welfare? For whom is pride not a cause of downfall? And for whom is humility not for their exaltation? (KDarp 1.32)

What is the use of a generous man if he is poor? What is the use of one of noble birth if he is a sinner? What is the use of a miser if he is contented? And what is the use of a wise man if he is blinded by pride? (KDarp 1.33)
For one who is overwhelmed by the demon of pride, friendship turns into enmity, giving turns into seizing,
and knowledge turns into a hundredfold ignorance.
Envy is the enemy of the virtuous; the excessive beggar is the enemy of the greedy;
everyone is an enemy to those who are arrogant, but no one is an enemy to those who speak kindly.
Therefore, my son, you must never harbor egoism;
for one whose neck is upraised with pride is surely seized by the fierce crocodile of delusion.
Whether it be through a noble lineage distinguished by its excellence, a multitude of virtues that are inwardly wondrous, a form exceedingly captivating, great wealth, or conduct—
whenever the great tree of delusion, consisting of intoxication, begins to grow, you must first apply yourself with effort to uprooting its firmly established foundation.
O son, even if you have attained prosperity, do not show disregard for virtues;
for even a jar that is completely full falls down from a well if its rope is severed.
Abandon pride in your lineage, which is merely a conventional pinnacle; abandon pride in wealth, which is seen and then lost.
Abandon pride in learning, which is like a commodity for sale; abandon pride in physical beauty, which is licked away by time.
My son, though you have been awakened by my efforts, if you do not abandon this pride and delusion,
then this conceit— producing intense torment— will become like a piercing thorn for you.
Arrogance is an elephant to the lotus of prosperity, a guide to the path where the thunderbolt falls to shatter the pride of the virtuous, and a rising column of smoke from the fire of merit.
It is a fresh fever for the beds of others and a cloud that obscures the lunar orb of one's conduct; it is always the cause of the destruction of the virtues of those with intoxicated minds.

If this impermanence were permanence, or if everything did not turn bitter upon cooking, then this pride of yours regarding lineage, wealth, learning, and so forth would not be a mockery. (KDarp 1.42)
"I am a debater, a master of learned knowledge among all scholars; I am proud, a fine poet through the ripening of the flow of my speech;
I am a playful swan wandering the Mānasa lake of lotus-eyed women"—thus does the demon of pride take root within men.
Fortune, though guarded, perishes in an instant; the body, too, is merely a collection of a multitude of calamities.
Even the attainment of pleasure through the union of enjoyment is unreal; this dense cloud of false pride is a curse.
Although addressed thus repeatedly by his father, he went off with eyes closed in playfulness,
like a rutting elephant rushing with speed, disregarding the goad.
Intoxicated with pride, they scratch the earth with their feet; sighing hot with anger, they make their faces terrifying with the knitting of brows and sidelong, crooked glances.

With the friction of their perspiring finger-joints against their foreheads, causing the skin of their brows to ache, they tremble at the time of hearing advice for their own benefit like those possessed by demons.
Once, while excellent horses were standing by, out of curiosity for their speed, he set out for his friend’s house during a festival, having mounted a donkey.
Goaded again and again by that sharp goad,
the donkey became afflicted with intense pain, drenched in flowing blood.
With tears streaming from his eyes and having recounted his sufferings through signs appropriate to his own species,
he spoke to his mother, the she-ass, who had come before him.
"O Mother, look at this son of a Brahmin, who possesses such a base disposition;
while I am pulling [the cart], he seeks to strike me, lashing me with a goad."
"What shall I do? I have been seized by this evil-minded Yama;
shall I cast him into a pit, or throw his body into a chasm?"

Then the female donkey, her eyes filled with tears, spoke with great distress to her son who was crying out thus, as if her own affection had been transferred to him: KDarp_1.52: "Then the female donkey, her eyes filled with tears, spoke with great distress to her son who was crying out thus, as if her own affection had been transferred to him."
O son, endure this intoxicating man; withstand his cruel affliction.
In his heart of cruel wood, there is not even a single grain of compassion.
Born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, this Raudra is devoid of Brahmanic virtue;
he knows not the suffering of others, being fierce and behaving like a Caṇḍāla.
A heart impoverished of compassion and speech as harsh as a saw—
this is the manifest characteristic of those born from a mixture of castes.
The speech of those born from a single seed is like fresh butter, their minds are tender with compassion, and their heads are bowed in humility.
The wicked man bellows with bitter arrogance out of anger, harboring enmity without cause; being of base birth, he feels no compassion for one fallen into misery;
fickle and delighting in momentary pleasures, he insults those who serve him; and with his neck held high, he utters outbursts of pride toward the virtuous.
Having heard these unbearable words of the female donkey, the twice-born man,
who was skilled in discerning the cries of all living beings, fell down, struck by utter bewilderment.
Having regained consciousness after a long time, like one fallen from the peak of Mount Meru,
he suddenly cast off his pride, as all the glory of his lineage had perished.
As if stunned by poison, he went to his mother's side;
having reported everything to her exactly as he had heard it, he questioned her in private.
Questioned by him as he was intent on renouncing his body,
and bound by an oath, she spoke to him with her face cast down, her words faltering with embarrassment.
How can I describe to you that shameful and ignoble act? Even within saṃsāra, the conduct of women is mysterious and full of wonder.
The mind of a woman is as fickle as the tip of an elephant's ear, as the leaf of a peepal tree, and as the flickering of lightning.
Women who are intent on virtue and self-sacrifice cannot be constrained by the qualities of their husbands, nor can they be detected by investigators, nor can they be turned back by wealth.
By whom can women—who are like rivers fallen from their heights, overwhelmed by the turbidity of pride born of wealth and youth—be restrained? (KDarp 1.65)
Those who sacrifice their bodies and take away the lives of men, though timid by nature, enter the fire;
those who are cruel yet possess limbs as delicate as young shoots deceive even the most discerning, for they are charmingly artful.
Long ago, at the time when the sky was marked by blossoming flowers, I stood alone in a flower grove, bathed in the dust of passion and intoxicated by youth.
While my husband was intent upon his initiation for the vow, I, with face downcast as if out of jealousy,
placed my hands upon my uplifted breasts and reflected for a long time.
Trembling with the wind, yawning,
and stained with the pollen of flowers, these creepers seem to sing with longing to the sounds of the bees.
Overcome by blossoming youth, yet deprived of the enjoyment of my beloved,
I have become fruitless solely through the fault of my husband, who persists in his vows.
At that moment of reflection, a barber named Parihāsa, holding a mirror before him,
arrived like a personification of the enemy of virtuous conduct.
Seeing me alone, distressed by the loss of my modesty,
he touched me as I trembled, with the playful gesture of grasping my toenails.
There, having completed my duties, I fainted with shame at the thought of associating with the base, looking down as if beholding my own fallen virtue.
Moving nearby, that she-ass saw all of that;
and this act of mine, which brings about a hidden pregnancy, is a sin against my lineage.
"Enough, my son, with this discussion of secret affairs;
it is only when things have been accomplished that bodies and families truly shine."
Having heard these words of his mother, he suddenly fell into blindness;
due to the descent of his birth-attained [vision], he became as if lifeless.
Then, having gone there, fasting and placing his hope in Brahmanhood, he performed austerities for a very long time on Mount Kailāsa, which laughs aloud with its peaks.
Pleased by his fierce asceticism, Śatakratu himself did not grant the status of a Brahmin to him who was begging for it, though it is difficult to obtain on earth.
Again and again, having scorched the three worlds with his asceticism,
he obtained divinity from the boon of the Thousand-Eyed One, but not the status of a Brahmin.
Then he became renowned on earth by the name Chandodeva,
to be worshipped for one day every year by women with deer-like eyes.
Since it is like a vast serpent in the underworld of delusion, one should not harbor pride regarding one's family or caste;
for they declare that noble character—consisting of tranquility, forbearance, generosity, and compassion—is true nobility.
He who has no mother that is a mass of lack of discernment, no father that is the ocean of rebirth,
and no beloved wife that is craving— he alone in this world is truly well-born and virtuous.
The second reflection:
Why this pride in wealth for men, which is as flickering as the corner of a goddess’s sidelong glance;
for even when bound around one's neck, it does not follow even a single step behind one who has passed away.
Wealth remains well-guarded when it is signless, and it remains unguarded by the turn of fate;
yet the wealth of a miser, even when being enjoyed, is like the dancing of a madman.
For men who rush about every morning with their labors, talk, and diversions, and who cry out "Wealth! Wealth!", death has been forgotten.
What distinction is there between a miser and a pauper— both of whom are lusterless and penniless, whose wives are tormented by hardship, and who alike suffer from the defect of affliction?
Those who, girded for the seizing of wealth, do not perceive the limit of death,
and who revile the greediness of others— it is they whose wealth others enjoy in the end.
The wealth of the rich, when spoken of to others, becomes an object of contempt; when left unsaid, it passes into invisibility;
and within the heart, it bears the nature of a thorn—until death.
Like one whose life-breath is at his throat, the afflicted man gazes upon the faces of his kinsmen with his wealth, which remains unrevealed even at the very end.
May that wealth belong to no one— wealth acquired through great hardships, wealth that is not enjoyed while living, and wealth which another shares at the end.
Knowledge leads to dispute, wealth to pride, excellence of wisdom to the deception of others, and extreme loftiness to defeat by the world; for those who possess these, light is indeed darkness.
For the miserly, internal thirst remains unappeased by the contact with the salt-water of wealth; their bodies lose their luster through long-term consumption of tasteless and parching food;
they suffer from insomnia and a sluggish digestive fire due to the constant fear of kings, water, thieves, and fire—this misery is clearly far greater than the suffering of the destitute.
In Śrāvastī there was a caravan leader named Nanda, who was like another Arthanātha; yet he brought no joy even to those who sought his favor through his fame.
That miser was always unbearable and a source of anxiety to all people;
he remained upon the heads of treasures like a venomous serpent waiting for its time.
Having spent the entire day counting the multitude of jars containing his hoard of wealth,
he eats at night— his habit being to consume no more than a handful of parched grain— his belly aching with pain.
Devoid of condiments, lacking salt, ruined, with its cooking unrefined, and beset by misery;
without a smile seen due to the cessation of expenditure, his house became silent with grief.
Lusterless, devoid of pleasure and joy, without lamps and destitute of water—
such was the home of that miser in the next world.

Though he constantly accumulated stores of food, he himself remained without food due to his chronic illnesses; though possessing gold, he became pale; and though surrounded by abundance, he grew emaciated with anxiety.
By a reversal of fate, that woman named Mati— attainable only through merit and appearing like the prosperity of wealth incarnate— became the wife of that unworthy man.
Always concealing [her wealth], she performed hospitality for her husband's guests;
because of that, she was consumed by the fire of quarrels during disputes over expenditures.
To her was born a virtuous son named Candana;
yet, by his father—who was blinded by the darkness of greed—he was led to a state other than his true nature, like a lotus [dragged] elsewhere.
Once, seeing a supplicant at the door of his own house who had obtained food elsewhere,
Nanda engaged in a quarrel with his wife that resulted in the shedding of blood.
With his lips bitten in rage and sighing, he spoke to his wife, who stood with her face cast down as if washing away the sin of that touch from her breasts with her tears.
"Who will give alms to me, whose wealth has been exhausted by your hand, since you, an ill-fated woman who brings poverty, reside in my house? (KDarp 2.22)
Where women act with audacity, concealing the agency of their husband,
that household will inevitably become the abode of supreme calamities.
A single house belongs to a householder; a hundred houses belong to one who seeks wealth.
For a master of the home whose riches have been consumed by his wife, all hope for the future is lost.
That wealth which provides satisfaction even by its mere sight and is the very life of living beings—
those who protect it consume their own bodies.

In this world, for embodied beings, poverty is death; though living, one who is inactive and destitute is like a corpse, whereas even a corpse is active through its wealth. For the poor, wealth is life itself.
This very power of the object is perceived through direct perception:
that while those still living carry a corpse on a palanquin, it is supported by the bond of the aggregates.
Why do you give food accumulated through hardship to those who beg?
For if that which is given is indeed for the sake of attainment, why is it not preserved once attained?
The connection with sons, wife, and others for men is rooted in wealth;
when that wealth is exhausted, sons flee and wives go elsewhere.
The wise, the poets, the heroes, the artists, and the ascetics all look toward the face of a wealthy physician, just as those who are ill look toward a doctor possessed of medical knowledge.
Having heard these words of that pitiable man, which were devoid of compassion for his interests,
she spoke to him in a manner befitting her own character and noble birth.
The virtuous strive diligently to acquire wealth for the sake of dharma;
for those disciplined in the practice of dharma, wealth is merely a collection of impurities.
That which produces aversion, affliction, craving, delusion, and sleeplessness—that is not wealth for the miserly; it is merely a disease of the heart.
The disease of wealth that increases only to cause separation from happiness and enjoyment finds its swift pacification through the treatment of the royal physician, the Path.
Due to greed, there was never any festival in his house;
at his death, those who share in his wealth dance to the beat of drums.
You carefully guard the grains, the rinsings, the husks, and the embers,
yet you do not perceive the heap of jewels stolen by mice within your treasury.
What indeed is this pride born of wealth, which perishes in an instant—
though it is being guarded, it is consumed by expenditure and overwhelmed by calamities?
When examined in accordance with reality, since human beings are subject to destiny,
greed for wealth is not praised in any circumstance whatsoever.
In an age of Kali, when friends are wicked, sons are beset by evil vices, thieves have multiplied, and the king is greedy— what is the use of wealth?

What is the use of wealth to one who is constantly at odds with creditors, whose virtues are severed by the passage of time, who hates giving, who is childless, and who has a weak digestion? (KDarp 2.40)
For one who has suddenly acquired wealth through crimes such as treason against the king,
what is the use of that fortune— which, due to fear, cannot be spent— any more than a thorn?

What is the use of the wealth of a rogue who is trusted as a friend, yet whose lofty virtues and splendor have been swallowed by the village of terrible misappropriations, and who is ignorant of how to distribute it?
For one who has exhausted himself in night-long service, who endures cold, wind, and heat,
who delights in the glance of his master, and who deserves only hardship— what is the use of wealth?

What is the use of wealth for one whose intellect is destroyed, who is satisfied by what is seen on birch bark, and who is intent upon acquiring wealth from every quarter out of greed for abundant gain?
Of what use is the wealth of a merchant of impure character, who is spat upon with loathing,
like the scent of cooking garlic, which is itself impure?
What is the use of wealth to one whose body is worn out by old age— wealth which, though desired and yet unobtained, was once fit for enjoyment during the prime of youth, but now acts like a burden?
For one who has renounced the household life through ordination, what is the use of wealth—which is like a bond—that acquires its purpose only through the honor and worship of people? (KDarp 2.47)
What is the use of wealth— which, like a dream, perishes in an instant— to a youth who, devoid of self-restraint, has been cast onto the wrong path by rogues?
What is the use of wealth acquired through sin by a village official who is forcibly enjoyed by a wife acting according to her own will?

For a guru who has attained perfection through the complete abundance of enjoyments, garments, and other riches provided by his disciples, what is the use of accumulated wealth acquired through deceit?
For one appointed to the royal treasury who is suspected solely on the grounds of signs of theft,
what is the use of wealth, which is like execution itself?
What is the use of the wealth of an astrologer in this world— a wealth that is constantly perishing due to faults such as the theft of ignorance, and which serves only as a cause for ridicule?
What is the use of wealth to a villager who eats boiled vegetables, like a full basket being squeezed by a king? (KDarp 2.53)
What is the use of wealth to a scribe who has stepped upon the world, who is as black as ink, a serpent bound at its neck? (KDarp 2.54)

Of one who is fierce in quarreling with his wife, who repeatedly disregards even a blade of grass [as insignificant], and who is tormented by anger, fasting, and sighs—what is the use of wealth? (KDarp 2.55)
Of what use is wealth to a miser who wears soiled and poor clothing, who subsists on meager food, and who suffers the extreme misery of poverty?
The poor are seen to be happy, while the wealthy are exceedingly miserable;
since the arising of happiness and suffering for living beings depends on destiny, what is the use of wealth?

When one's kinsmen have passed away and all things are equalized, what is the use of wealth for one whose mind is vacant and who is disenchanted with this tasteless and essence-less cycle of existence?
For the wise man who is free from anxiety regarding the purpose he has already attained and utilized,
and who is content with even the slightest gain— what use has he for wealth?
The fool views grass and gold with an equal eye; lacking discernment, he does not recognize what is beneficial regarding sense objects.
At that time, when his treasury is filled with wealth sufficient for its maintenance, tell me, what can one devoid of discrimination do?

When an embodied being, rendered helpless by grief, laments the sudden separation from a friend dearer than life, a young woman, or a son who is a treasury of virtues— tell me then, what can he do even with mountains of jewels?

When an old man has become as inert as the wind, he hears no purpose, nor does he seek stability; he perceives neither touch, nor taste, nor even fragrance. Tell me then, what can he do with enjoyments or wealth?
Afflicted by disease, a living being does not even look upon food with his eyes; tormented by intense pain, he longs for death.
When all medicines have failed and he cries out in distress, tell me, what can he do then with grain and wealth?
With his kinsmen distressed by the loss of sleep, abandoned by the anxious physician, tormented by the decoctions of digestion, agitated by the attendants out of fear of his lethargy,
his hopes for health shattered, and his two feet gripped by his beloved— who at the end of his life does a man gain by wealth that is like a thorn?
Adorned with precious gems worth ten million gold pieces and with elephants and horses as his mounts,
one does not find life for even a moment when seized by Time at its appointed hour, like a peacock's tail-feather.

Devoid of consciousness, his body like a piece of wood, abandoned in an instant by sons, wife, and friends, and subject to the fruits of his own past good and evil deeds—tell me, what can he do with the jewels acquired through great effort? (KDarp 2.66)

Therefore, do not become possessed by pride through the delusion arising from abundant wealth, as if you were overcome by a demon; for these glories, which are like flashes of lightning amidst the thick darkness of powerful greed, vanish in an instant.
When their wealth and sovereignty were lost, it is heard that Nala, Rāma, and the sons of Pāṇḍu formerly entered the forest in distress;
Śakra, deprived of his glory, entered the hollow of a lotus stalk out of shame. Who, then, can place their trust in wealth, which is so fickle despite its various methods of acquisition?
Although addressed thus repeatedly by his wife, he did not waver from his greed;
for by whom can the innate nature of all living beings be restrained?
Then, in the course of time, that physician, devoid of medical skill due to greed,
died with his back stuck inside a treasure jar in the treasury.
Having abandoned wealth that was long protected yet never enjoyed because it was not given away,
miserly men go to their destruction in their own homes, just like mice.
When he had departed for hell, the king took his wealth;
in the end, the riches of the greedy belong to the king.
Then, for Candana, the son of that [king], there occurred a great festival of expenditure involving vast quantities of wealth, even with the remainder of what had been left over.
"Let no one here speak of Nanda’s meager fire out of fear of the ruin of his enjoyments"— thus did the people say there in the morning.
"Fie, fie on wealth! It is a base wealth, like that of Nanda, which only brings suffering to oneself!
Thus spoke the city-dwellers: "Let everything be given away; let everything be enjoyed!"
Then, when her time had come, the old and blind Caṇḍālī woman named Khaṇḍikā, who lived within the outer courtyard gate, gave birth to a son.
Blind, humpbacked, emaciated, lame, leprous, and with a thick, constricted throat—he was like a collection of miseries; such was her son.
When his mother’s milk was exhausted due to his lack of merit, he remained motionless;
then, out of compassion, he was raised on the milk of a female dog by the women of his kin.
This very diversity of past actions is what causes those who are oppressed by hardship to live on, while even the powerful perish.
Covered with wounds teeming with swarms of worms rotting in putrid filth, he lay like a corpse in a hamlet upon a bed of damp grass.
Out of excessive affection for him, his mother fixed her steady attachment upon her son;
for the delusion of love, when embedded in latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), is indeed difficult to endure.
Growing up gradually, grey as the charcoal of a cremation ground,
he became a source of terror even to the fierce piśācas of the outcaste hamlets.
Moving with a cane and loathsome due to the moisture of leprosy,
he went along that path by which no other person had traveled.
In the meantime, on the day of the funeral rites for Candana’s father,
there arose a great clamor from the multitude of supplicants as food was being distributed.
Then, taking up a skull-bowl, that young outcaste slowly approached the ground before the door, begging for water for rinsing his mouth with great difficulty.
Seeing him defiling the path of the brahmins from the palace roof, Candana said in anger: "Let this man who has arrived be quickly driven away! (KDarp 2.86)
Then, struck by the gatekeeper with a staff out of fear of the Lord’s frown,
he whirled around like a pigeon.
With the bone of his forehead shattered and drenched by the flowing blood,
he fainted for a moment and then regained his life to experience the fruits of his afflictions.
Hearing that cry, the Caṇḍālī woman, who was nearby,
approached and lamented in distress, touching his blood.
Alas, by what merciless one has this manly prowess been displayed,
whereby even with a mangled and dripping body, he has acted like a great warrior in this place?
Having seen this unbearable state of suffering consisting of bodily evil,
who, at such an occasion for detachment, has committed such cruelty?
Seeing such distress of his, which causes the heart to wither, who would commit a sin? For sin is indeed the very footstep of calamities.
If he did not commit great sin in a previous birth,
then tell me, for whose sake has such a state— so full of throbbing pain— been seen?
Those very ones who are seen to cause the particular, harsh pains of calamity and affliction are themselves the gurus for men in the act of sowing the seeds of sin.
Who can count the sins of the brave toward those worthy of compassion, of enemies toward their benefactors, and of deceivers toward the innocent? (KDarp 2.95)
"Why do you cry out so loudly, my son? Endure this pain born of the blow;
it is the creation of unwholesome karma, cutting to the quick of all embodied beings."
While she was thus lamenting and the assembled people were looking on, the Jina,
the kinsman of the helpless and an ocean of compassion, proceeded along that path.
To those exhausted by the wanderings of existence and tormented by the defects of passion and the like,
he seemed to anoint the heavens with the sandalwood paste of his splendor— an ointment akin to nectar, providing them with consolation.
Seeing him fallen into calamity, broken by a terrible disease, submerged in misfortune, and distressed,
the Blessed Lord of Jinas, moistened with the essence of compassion, reached out his hand to soothe his suffering.
By his mere presence, he became free from distress for a moment and attained, as it were, a state of well-being;
for the sight of those whose intentions are set on the welfare of beings destroys evil and gives birth to virtue.
Then, having learned that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, had arrived— smiling like a blossoming flower— Candana went forth, taking offerings for worship.
The Blessed One also, having ascended a golden lotus that had emerged from the earth due to his wondrous power, remained seated in the playful posture of the paryaṅka.
The Blessed One, pleased, spoke to Candana in the assembly of monks— he who stood before him, bowing with his head at the feet and with his hands busily engaged in worship.
Why was this wretched man beaten in anger even as he begged?
Why was your heart, so tender with compassion, not directed toward this miserable creature?
Those whose intentions are pure become moist with compassion toward all sentient beings;
for such as these, it is a defiled mind that is the cause of sufferings such as these.
Even toward those who have committed cruel injuries and are harsh with hatred,
the virtuous do not become callous, though they may be withered by the heat of the afflictions.
Alas, this wretched miser, afflicted by greed in another life,
is now tormented by bodily suffering as he prepares to give nothing away.
"This is Nanda, your father; because of a heap of impurities that had reached its full measure, he was shrouded by the disease of sin and attained the state of a caṇḍāla."
Therefore, because he was on the verge of death due to a disease even in another birth, gold was given by him; by that act, he became wealthy.
Whatever one who is about to die bestows at the stage of their final afflictions becomes unenjoyable for them due to greed in other future births.

No wealth was given for the sake of compassion; rather, the mind was set entirely upon the pursuit of greed. Those who have danced with the pleasures of accumulating hoards now grieve over their own sinful conduct.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One delivered a meritorious discourse on the Dharma,
by which Candana attained the state of an Arhat, worthy of the abandonment of the afflictions.
Therefore, a man should not give way to pride as his wealth increases;
for wealth that is neither given away nor enjoyed is an ill omen for men, both in this world and the next.
If knowledge produces pride and delusion— which is the sole cause for the pacification of the defects of cyclic existence—
it will certainly lead to blinding darkness, like a garland of rays from the sun in a cloudy sky. (KDarp 3.1)
Even birds can recite with great clarity through the practice of training;
what is this pride in knowledge when only a single portion has been painfully acquired?
That is true knowledge which destroys pride; that is prosperity which rains down upon those in need;
and that is called wisdom which follows the path of Dharma.
Salutation to that fool who is a scholar in name only, whose nature is perverted, and who brings his teacher of knowledge into contempt through the corruption of his conduct. KDarp_3.4 //
Alas, that fool who, having acquired knowledge, makes his mind turbid with hatred, has— by that very act— covered himself in dust after having bathed.
Like the goddess Śrī, learning falls into contempt through greed and hatred;
it shines only through humility, like a woman of noble family through her modesty.
The learning of the virtuous, characterized by contentment,
remains desirable only so long as it has not been displayed in the marketplace of the royal court.
The six virtues remain pure only so long as they have not been washed with the cleansing waters of debate and examined by the wicked in the assembly of kings.
Even a stone that is heartless examines the essence of one's virtues; for such a person, a desire to fall into fire is as appropriate as it is for gold.
By poets, their speech— captivating with its various ornaments— is made a tool for the benefit of others through greed, just as a courtesan is employed for the service of kings.
The speech of disputants, harsh through contact with logic that results in strife,
has fallen like the edge of a saw upon the root of Dharma.
The speech of the cruel disputants has been made harsh by logicians solely to destroy the splendor of the virtuous, like a butcher’s knife used by butchers.
He does not maintain moral conduct, nor does he fix his mind on the Dharma that is pure with fame; out of envy, he spreads the fault of harshness through his speech toward the wise.

By means of dialectical arguments, he generally reduces the actions pertaining to the next world to a state of doubt. What is the use of learning for that fool, so skilled at fruitlessly tearing apart the scriptures?
Those who, disputing in assemblies, are pierced by the thorn of another’s fame and strive to conceal the virtues of the virtuous by praising their own qualities—

their knowledge, like the blazing crest-jewel of black serpents, becomes a source of terror to the people, for their inner vision is clouded by the dregs of anger and they breathe out the heat of hatred.
Through lack of moral conduct one becomes an object of pity; through hatred, one becomes impure;
and knowledge, struck down by pride, perishes along with one's very life. (KDarp 3.15)
In ancient times, two excellent sages, Raibhya and Bharadvāja— honored by the wise among sages— established themselves as friends in a penance grove.
Raibhya had two sons, Sarvāvasu and Parāvasu, who were like stainless mirrors of knowledge and were envied by those who recognize virtue.
Bharadvāja had a son named Yavakrīta;
sons such as these, generally cherished by their fathers' affection, become proficient in learning.
Seeing those two sons of Raibhya, who were renowned everywhere for their learning,
that youth became filled with envy and was overwhelmed with remorse.
Having gone to the bank of the Jahnavi, emaciated by fasting for a long time,
he performed intense austerity with an immovable body in order to acquire the vidyās.
To him, whose soul was refined by asceticism, Śatakratu himself approached and said:
"O son of a sage, what is this futile persistence of yours?"
How can knowledge be acquired without having studied it from the mouth of a teacher?
Scholarship without practice is like a crown made of sky-flowers.
Now, what use is knowledge to you, since childhood—the proper time for knowledge—has passed?
Be attentive toward that which is indeed the fruit of knowledge.
Virtue, devotion to the welfare of others, humility, forbearance, fortitude,
and non-attachment— these are the radiant fruits of the ripening of knowledge.
Knowledge devoid of discernment, withered by the heat of hatred and anger,
is as fruitless as a creeper struck down by the thunderbolt of pride.
Corrupted by hatred, he applies his intellect to the sacred scriptures for this purpose:
"By means of these disputes, I shall cause the pride of the wise to wither. (KDarp 3.26)
Having abandoned tranquility and contentment— the first fruits of true knowledge—
those who seek the fruit of wealth travel by various mistaken paths.
What is the use of that knowledge which is a burden—accumulated through heaps of books—and which provides no benefit to others nor to oneself? (KDarp 3.28)
What is the use of that base artifice by which injustice is led to the status of justice through bold assertion, and justice is led to the status of injustice through greed? (KDarp 3.29)
What is the use of that impudent learning which is constantly made to expose itself in the midst of the assembly, like a wife whose garments have been pulled away by the praises of her own tongue?
What is the use of that parrot-like learning which, devoid of practice and consisting merely of rote recitation, only serves to delight the world?
What is the use of that deceitful knowledge which is concealed from one who possesses scriptural learning, yet revealed before a fool, and which is not imparted to disciples? (KDarp 3.32)
What is the use of that "merchandise of knowledge" which, having concealed the excellence of others, is spread out for sale before the wealthy again and again?
Of what use is that delusive ignorance which constantly clings to the mind, by means of which this terrible ocean of saṃsāra, filled with sea-monsters, cannot be crossed?
What is the use of that painful learning which, through the effort of constant practice, exhausts one's life while obstructing the three goals of human existence?
What is the use of that dull ignorance which does not produce in men an intellect suited for discernment nor a mind filled with dispassion?
Of what use is that science of hypocrisy, which is joined with false pride and by which the status of a Vedic scholar is abandoned through disputes over purity and impurity? (KDarp 3.37)
What is the use of that knowledge of surgery which causes pain through the thorn of supreme envy and robs one of pleasant sleep? It is merely a science of agony.
What is the use of that thief-like science by which one’s own excellence is proclaimed through the theft of another's hymns and the mere recitation of what has been spoken by a sister?
What is the use of that dull-witted learning which, its enthusiasm destroyed by lack of practice, is overcome by others; which, out of stupidity, produces only shame? (KDarp 3.40)
What is the use of that false knowledge which neither brings peace to one possessed of abundant wealth nor to a renunciant whose passion persists? (KDarp 3.41)
Of what use is that knowledge of faults which, by relying on a king, causes one to disparage the virtues of others and destroys their gifts, honor, and prosperity? (KDarp 3.42)
What is the use of that "muted learning" which, though it flows like a continuous stream at home, fails to manifest in an assembly due to the obstruction of one's presence of mind? (KDarp 3.43)
What is the use of that science of slaughter by which a battle is provoked— like [the barking] of fierce dogs, greedy for morsels and full of hatred and malice?
What is the use of that dead lore which, having been repeated over and over at the throat of the arrogant man, has been forgotten— like the dwindling life-force of one who has perished?
What is the use of that science of laughter, by which a physician treats one worn out by old age, a chronic patient, an alchemist, or a pauper? (KDarp 3.46)
Of what use is that science of the hunter, which relies on the snares of hope and by means of deceptive traps afflicts bewildered deer with piercing arrows?
What is the use of that deceptive science which follows mechanical diagrams and mantras, by means of which one inflicts injury upon others through fraudulent spells for subjugation and the like?
A teacher is excluded from that knowledge by pride, a poet by hatred, an ascetic by the pursuit of enjoyments, a king by sin, and a twice-born man by anger. (KDarp 3.49)
Those qualities of knowledge belonging to the learned which are rooted in discernment are true virtues;
all others, being equivalent to mere minor arts and crafts, are merely means of livelihood.
Like a lute to one who lacks ears, like a tremulous-eyed woman to one who is blind,
or like a garland of flowers to one who is dead, knowledge is fruitless for the arrogant.
What is the use of the life of those whose learning is destroyed by hatred and pride, whose intellect is destroyed by lust and anger,
and whose conduct is destroyed by greed and delusion?
Set aside that difficult grammar which agitates the elements and exhausts the body; the tasteless Mīmāṃsā does not wither you—enough with those harsh logics!
One does not fall intoxicated by the new poetic wines that cause the delusions of passion; therefore, for the eternal welfare of those with peaceful minds, dispassion is the giver of health.
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, he did not waver from his resolve;
for the stubborn persistence of those seized by pride is indeed difficult to restrain.
Then, having become an aged brahmin, Śakra began slowly to construct a bridge across the Gaṅgā with handfuls of sand.

Seeing him motionless, his afflictions fruitless and his efforts rendered vain, the son of the Sage approached him and, filled with compassion, asked with a smile: *taṃ dṛṣṭvā niṣphalakleśa-viphalodyoganiścalam / munisūnuḥ kṛpāviṣṭaḥ papracchābhyetya sasmitaḥ //* KDarp_3.56 //
"O Brahmin, why this persistence of yours in a futile endeavor?
Wise men do not perform actions that are fruitless and involve great exertion."
In these waters, agitated by the tossing of crooked waves,
how could a bridge made of handfuls of sand ever become a cause for laughter?
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, the brahmin said to him:
"Aha! Everyone becomes a scholar when it comes to advising others."
"You wish to obtain by means of asceticism knowledge that you have not studied;
just as your undertaking is fruitless, so too am I another fool."
Having heard these words of the twice-born man, which were indeed true, he was silenced in his reply;
nevertheless, firm in his resolve, he did not waver from his duty.
Then, by virtue of his intense asceticism, Śakra granted him an excellent boon,
by which he instantly became a treasury of all branches of knowledge.
Having acquired his learning, he went quickly and full of enthusiasm to his own hermitage,
and related to his father the account of the attainment of the fruits of his asceticism.
To him, who was overcome by intoxication yet spoke in refined Sanskrit with tireless eloquence,
Bharadvāja spoke as if agitated by perspiration, even though he himself was filled with joy.
"My son, you have acquired knowledge; why then do you speak of the heat of asceticism?
Because of fear for the future, this [renunciation] does not seem right to me."
Nearby here is the penance grove of the irascible Raibhya;
his two sons, Arvāvasu and Parāvasu, are blinded by the intoxication of their learning.
Both you and he are intoxicated by tireless learning and are newly risen scholars;
therefore, in their association, the Kali age, consisting of hatred, is ever present.
With his neck stiffened, suffering from headaches at the mere mention of another's excellence, his state overwhelmed by anxious wandering, delirium,

and intense agitation, and sighing hot with the fever of uneven anger born from the entry of the poison of internal hatred— the transformation of the new scholar is indeed painful, the ground for the onset of a terrifying fever.
When you have gone there, O sage, as you debate what is proper and improper,
my subjugation will inevitably come about through your curse.
The demoness of the pride of learning surely produces madness through the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl and the perception of blue, yellow, and other such colors. (KDarp 3.70)
This destruction was sought by you through the instruction of secret spells;
if my word is to be followed, you must not go to Raibhya’s hermitage.
Although addressed thus repeatedly by his father, he went to the two sons of Raibhya and constantly brought about the destruction of their pride in learning through the exhaustion of their disputes.
To him, who was intoxicated with pride, those two— whose faces were made hideous by angry and terrifying frowns,
and who were pierced by the thorn of hatred for the sciences that resided in his mind— spoke.
Since you, though younger than us both in age and in learning,
insult us with your words, may your life be shortened accordingly.
Although addressed thus by the two of them in anger, he did not desist out of pride;
for those arrogant with intoxication take no account of whether one is pleased or enraged.
In the meantime, the season of flowers— the time of death for those whose beloveds were away— arrived, possessing the playful charm of arched brows formed by swarms of wandering bees.
With their petals scattered and their eyes clouded by the pollen of flowers,
the Malaya breezes moved as if they were scholars filled with resentment.
Through the repeated play of their voices, which were sweet, charming, and noble,
a rivalry arose among the cuckoos as if among poets.
When Raibhya had departed with his two sons to bathe at the riverbank,
Bharadvāja’s son arrived and entered that hermitage.
There he beheld Purūravas’s lawful wife, named Suprabhā, who was intent on gathering flowers and who surpassed even Rati in the pride of her beauty.
She was receiving instruction in the art of graceful movement from the doe-like glances of the does clinging to the courtyard of the hermitage,
as she herself moved with tremulous side-long looks.
Upon seeing her, whose face was like the moon and who was a goddess of delight for the god of love,
the son of the sage suddenly overstepped the bounds of propriety.
That celibate student, agitated by fresh desire,
spoke to her— even though he was unskilled in speaking words appropriate to his longing.
This form of yours, which intoxicates and is so well-suited to the Mind-born God,
makes my heart feel as if it is overflowing with passion.
Having cast aside learning and discipline, and having abandoned the restraints of my teacher,
my mind has turned toward you, bound by the affection of a previous birth.
I know that this is the fruit of the ripening of my past actions;
nevertheless, I am unable to restrain my desire—what can I do?
Neither by learning, nor by wealth, nor by conduct,
nor by ritual action can the mind, once set upon the path of passion, be restrained.
Having spoken thus to her, whose eyes were wandering in fear as she turned toward the hermitage and set out to depart,
he approached and seized her by the hem of her garment.
Being dragged with force by him into the desolate wilderness like a plantain tree by an elephant,
she spoke to him, her fingers moving in a gesture of prohibition.
Do not, do not defile my own pure character;
is this a fitting fruit for faultless knowledge?
Having cast aside modesty— your own wife, as it were, clothed in the white silken garment of virtue—
you seize with your hand the hem of the robe belonging to other women.
Seeing this unprecedented sight, "What is this? the water-pot surely gazes at your face with its neck upturned, as if out of curiosity.
Bearing the weight of matted hair and bark garments, which possess an inner luster like that of a fresh flower-arrowed god, your burden does not lead to peace, just as that of a tree does not.
Merely at the thought of an evil intention, she fell before you with her face cast down in shame;
her rosary of eyes trembled as if out of fear of your touch.
O Sarasvatī, whose lips quiver with the chanting of prayers while seated upon your lotus-throne—
this ill-conducted speech is not fitting for the mouth of a wise person such as yourself.
How is it that this ground of the penance grove, which engenders detachment, produces in you, who have not conquered yourself, a longing as if she were your own mother?
The intoxication of youth, like a horse that is difficult to tame, is a snatcher away;
it casts the person whose self is entirely slack into a pit in an instant.
Shame on this intellect! Of what use is discernment? Let sacred learning rest far away from those who do not restrain a mind that falters under the transformations of saṃsāra.
Where is learning— the intellect that discerns what ought and ought not to be done through the knowledge of all matters—
and where is folly, the consort of wicked deeds and great sins?
Even when addressed in this way, since he did not relinquish his stubborn grasp, she,
terrified that her virtue would be stolen away, then reflected:
"What shall I do, having been obtained by the heedless one in this desolate place, helpless as I am?
What will those who have abandoned the bartering of Dharma not do when left unchecked? (KDarp 3.101)
This man, afflicted by love, cannot be turned back by mere words;
those who are arrogant with passion, anger, and pride are deceived only by soothing speech.
Having reflected thus, she, speaking softly, said to him gently:
"Go; I myself shall come at night to the empty bower of creepers."
"Having bathed at this time, my father-in-law does not come with his son;
what will you do in the presence of him who is like a blazing fire?"
Thus addressed by her, he departed, having understood her words to be true;
for those deluded by passion consider even what is difficult to attain to be easily gained.
Then Raibhya arrived and stood before the fire-sanctuary;
his daughter-in-law spoke to him, raining down tears as if from the smoke of the fire of her wrath.
"O dear one, that wicked son of Bharadvāja, who is your friend's son,
has today approached me in this lonely place to violate my virtue at my request."
"I deceived him, who was seized by a malignant planet, saying 'I shall come';
otherwise, I would not have escaped from his grasp alive and well."
Having heard this, the sage suddenly blazed with wrath and became like the sun when it is cruelly eclipsed by the fall of a meteor— a portentous omen.
Discrimination flashes within those possessed of true knowledge whose minds are composed;
yet at the time of a crisis, delusion arises in their hearts, for knowledge remains only in the book.
Then, sighing deeply, his eyes reddened by the onset of the fever of anger,
he spoke with his lower lip trembling as if from the muttering of a malevolent spell:
Ah! How Bharadvāja exerted himself in providing religious instruction to his son, only to make that son—who had approached another’s wife—stand naked!
Having spoken thus, unable to say more due to the fury of his indignation,
he entered the fire-chamber and became intent on a remedy.
With a fierce and terrifying display of wrath, he plucked out his matted locks— tawny like a blazing fire—
and offered them as an oblation into the flames, as if they were the bristling mane of a cruelly angry lion.
And when the second oblation had been offered, the terrible Rākṣasa Śūlabhṛt appeared accompanied by Kṛtyās, and bowing down, he spoke to the sage: KDarp 3.115.
"What shall I do, O Sage? For whose destruction have I been created?
By your command, I am prepared to consume even the three worlds."
To him who was speaking thus, Raibhya addressed the son of Bharadvāja in a harsh manner: "Go, devour this fool! (KDarp 3.117).
Thus instructed by him, he went along, making the earth tremble;
seeing the son of the sage from afar performing his half-bath, he rushed toward him.
When that night-stalker rushed forward with speed, his flaming spear raised,
the son of the sage, his progress broken by fear, found no refuge.
Fleeing with speed, he reached his father’s hermitage;
as he was entering the fire-sanctuary, he was stopped by a Śūdra who was defiled by impurity.
Touched by the servant, he became impure and fell to the ground in agitation;
then, struck by the demon’s trident, he was suddenly reduced to ashes.
In the meantime, Bharadvāja, entering his own hermitage and observing that its splendor had vanished, became agitated and reflected:
The fires always rise before me when I return from gathering flowers and fruits; why are they as if motionless today?
Having reflected thus, and seeing his son before him terrified by the ashes,
and having heard the account related by the servant, the sage fell to the ground.
Having regained consciousness, he spoke slowly with a voice choked with tears:
"Let even the learned Raibhya meet his death at the hands of his own son in due time."
Alas, my son! Even though you were protected, I cannot live without you, any more than I could live with this body which, despite being guarded, is flawed and falls away in every moment.
Having spoken thus, the sage entered the fire of the funeral pyre out of grief for his son;
for even among the great, sorrows flow with unbroken force when they arise from a fresh cause.
Then, as time passed slowly, the two priests Arvāvasu and Parāvasu went to the palace of King Bṛhadyumna.
When that long sacrificial session of Pṛthuśrī had duly commenced,
an extraordinary outpouring of gifts and honors arose for those two officiating priests.
Once, at the end of the day during the twilight hour,
Parāvasu, while returning to his own hermitage, saw his father before him.
Overpowered by the curse, he mistook the black antelope skin draped over [the sage's] shoulder for a deer and struck him with his staff; by that act, he became unconscious.
Beholding Janaka slain and agitated by the fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin,
he went to the sacrificial ground and reported that matter to his brother.
Arvāvasu said to him, "Brother, what can be done against fate,
by whose mere will such reversals as these come to pass?"
One seeking dharma incurs sin; one seeking virtue suffers the ruin of virtue;
when fate has turned adverse, one seeking wealth falls into poverty.
"For your sake, I am performing this severe vow for the expiation of Brahmin-slaughter;
you, however, must complete the sacrificial rites for this lord of the earth."
Having spoken thus, Arvāvasu, firm in his vows, performed the completion of severe expiations at all the sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of pacifying his brother's sin.
When Parāvasu, the slayer of his father, learned from afar that he had completed his vow and arrived at King Yajñasena’s sacrificial grounds, he reflected thus:
"This man has come to take his share at the time of my sacrificial gift;
alas for my ill fortune, he lives on even though he has long been afflicted by the rigors of severe vows."
Having reflected thus, he approached the lord of the earth and spoke,
having fallen into the lap of greed and envy with a desire for sin.
"O King, this sinner, my brother, who has committed the murder of a Brahmin, enters the sacrificial ground without hesitation; let him be restrained from here."
Thus addressed by that ungrateful man, the king,
through his perversity and ignorance, prohibited the entrance of that sinless man.
Like the blind, they do not perceive what is appropriate or inappropriate, what is beneficial or harmful;
they travel by that very same path along which kings are led.
He did not become angry with his brother because of the gift of false slander;
for the wise consider destiny to be the cause of humiliation.
Delighted by his compassion and his unwavering composure,
the gods seated at the sacrifice spoke to him.
"O Sage, we are delighted by this tranquility of yours;
O you of excellent conduct, though you are worthy of a boon, please accept this most excellent boon."
Thus addressed by the gods with affection, he spoke to them with palms joined in reverence:
"If I am worthy of your favor, let that which I desire be granted to me."
May he who was slain by my father through malevolent magic— the son of Bharadvāja—
be restored to life, as shall his father, who inflicted that cruel injury upon him while he was unaware.
May our father, who was killed by Parāvasu under the mistaken belief that he was a deer,
now regain his life, restored to health and having forgotten that anger.
When he had thus requested this boon, those gods replied, "So be it";
Yavakrīta, Bharadvāja, and Raibhya then regained their own lives.
Thus, even these sages fell into a state of lamentation when their learning became fruitless through pride; when their discernment—its pure light destroyed by the blindness of anger—had fallen away;
and when their virtue had melted away through the great heat of passion and perished through hatred. For whom else, then, does knowledge provide any merit when it is soiled by the conceit of wealth?
For the sake of peace of mind, a wise person who has abandoned hatred and pride should exert effort in every way;
for the lamp of knowledge is of no use at all to those whose eyes are agitated by desire and anger, or who are blinded by arrogance.
Non-attachment is the supreme wealth; non-violence is the supreme austerity;
freedom from deceit is the supreme knowledge for the wise, being beyond reproach.
The learning of Śukra, who had amassed noble and manifold wealth, was pitiable as it served only to steal his riches and wife;
likewise, the learning of Kaca, though born of Vācaspati himself, was rendered fruitless through deceit.

The serpent of the Kali age, whose venom is hatred, does not touch the intellect of those whose minds are pure through tranquility, provided that pride does not arise within their own hearts. (KDarp 3.154) The Fourth Reflection.
What is this pride in the instability of their form among these men who are like lotuses and as beautiful as the day?
For those whose beauty and luster are merely momentary, like the turmeric dye upon garments.
By nature, her youthful body is like a painting lacking the division of lines and contours;
yet it attains full bloom through youth alone, just as a śirīṣa flower does through the festival of spring.
For a few days, the hairless face of young men possesses the splendor of the full moon;
but once the vast net of a beard has grown, it bears a resemblance to a lotus shrouded by moss.
As a painting by smoke, a lotus by frost, the orb of the moon by the dark fortnight,
water by the summer heat, and a beautiful form by the onset of old age, [he] does not shine.

Old age, like a courtesan, devours the wealth of people by seizing their hair; she is addicted to devouring the morsels of blood and flesh momentarily acquired by the form, through the uncaused fault of desire.

Through the very process of ripening, Time— possessing diverse karmic power, acting imperceptibly to embodied beings at every moment, and flowing with four currents— brings about beautiful and ugly forms by means of its power of transformation.
The movement of time is not perceived, yet it produces the illusion of a swiftly spinning wheel;
he who was a child yesterday is today in the full bloom of youth, and by morning that very same person will have a body worn out by old age.

Among the three stages of life divided into three parts for men, youth alone bestows beauty, and nothing else. When that youth is afflicted by defects such as intoxication, madness, disease, physical infirmity, and deformity, where is there any beauty?
When a man grieves, tormented by suffering, having abandoned food, his face discolored by sorrow;
when he neither bathes nor rises nor even lies down—then where is beauty, and where is the splendor of youth?

When one stands in prison like a ghost, reduced to mere bones, with grey hair standing on end and a body covered in scattered lice and dandruff— where then has the pride in one's physical beauty gone?

When one’s body is ruined by service and exile that constantly accepts the suffering of wretchedness, and when the knees are broken by the wandering of perpetual travel, then there is no longer any beauty for one who once possessed beauty.

When all his limbs are crushed by blows, his lips and nose severed, and his eyes and teeth shattered, even a youth attains a state like that of a Piśāca; at that time, too, beauty has lost its true nature.
When a wise man is not a destroyer of his enemies, nor eloquent in speech, and is merely like an ordinary person,
then it is better to be ugly yet possess a desirable form than to be handsome yet lacking in discernment.

When a poor man, lacking even clothing, makes an excessive plea while shrinking with shame, he appears utterly deformed despite his handsome features due to the wrinkles formed upon his cheeks. (KDarp 4.14)

In an assembly of scholars, he who is ignorant of languages and thus mocked by eminent poets and disputants with signs of praise for Śiva’s vehicle—the elephant—is like one sold in a foreign marketplace by rogues and left speechless; what is the use of the beauty of form for that man, whose body is merely as charming as a painted peacock?

Whose limbs do not grow weary at the sight of his form and body, as he drinks up time with the hollow of his hand formed by his fingers, and days and nights with the cupped palms of his hands? (KDarp 4.16)
The black bee of Time devours from all sides the form, youth, valor, the enjoyment of love, the power of wisdom, wealth, and the body of men, just as it consumes the filaments of lotuses.
Once, in the assembly hall, all the apsarases served the Lord of Śacī with dance and song together with the gandharvas.
Among them, the lovely Urvaśī shone like the Kaiśikī among the dramatic styles; she seemed to proclaim a friendship between the moon and the lotus with her own face.
Having come there for the service of Śakra, the gods, upon seeing that moon-faced woman,
considered themselves blessed, as she had become an integral part of the erotic sentiment.
Dancing, she shone, reflected in the central gems of the necklaces,
as if entering simultaneously into the hearts of the gods.
The swans, surpassed by her gait, lay dormant within the celestial chariots of the gods;
and the deer in the moon fell asleep for a moment, conquered by her side-long glances.
A garland of blue lotus petals, fallen from her crest upon her breasts, shone like a row of eyes of jealous Apsarases.

The mass of pearls, released from the breaking threads of necklaces tossed about by the whirls of her dancing as she was uplifted by her own energy, and appearing like a continuous stream of nectar-drops falling from the moon of her face, for a moment took on the beauty of the thick drops of perspiration arising from the exertion of her passion for the dance upon the slopes of her breasts.
Seeing her body bristling with horripilation as she watched the dance, Rati created a screen before Manmatha using the pollen from her beautiful form, which was intensified by her sighs.
Beholding even the succession of Hari’s eyes fixed there, Śacī became despondent; she created a darkness in the center with the bees hovering over the playful lotus shaken by her anger.
Did they not indeed create an obstacle for those meritorious men while they were witnessing the playful dance?
For their eyes, captivated by the form of Urvaśī, were devoid of even a blink.
There, the two Aśvins, the gods who were preeminent in the sweetness of their beauty—
A conversation took place between the two of them, whose hearts were drawn by his virtues.
One said: "Oh, the beauty of this tremulous-eyed woman!
By it even sages, though bound by their vows, have been thrown into agitation."
In this assembly, whose face will these glances of the noble-born woman fall upon— glances curved with the modesty born of shame at the disclosure of her amorous dalliance?
When two people of virtuous conduct gaze at one another,
the god of love bestows in secret that very deposit which is the essence of the erotic sentiment.
Whose neck will this tremulous-eyed woman, having emerged from the arena, longingly embrace with her arms—his body surrendered in battle? (KDarp 4.31)
To him who was speaking thus, another replied with a smile:
"Oh, have you forgotten Purūravas, the moon of the earth?"
His fame is sung in all directions as an ornament of valor, a tilaka of loveliness for the earth, and as something made auspicious by the enjoyment of Urvaśī.
By means of her beauty, virtues, and enthusiasm, this Urvaśī has been won over;
though she stands before Śakra, she dwells there in his mind.
Born of the lineage of the moon, he is ashamed because of his resemblance in form;
envious Smara does not speak of him in the presence of Rati.
Alas, I do not know what this perverse whim of the flower-bowed god is,
since he does not even place his five arrows into the hand of that very person.
We do not know how that slender woman does not dance at all, while she carries in her heart that playful lover who supports the entire earth girt by oceans and whose arms hang down to his knees.
That king should be sought out with effort, even at an improper time;
for who knows how long such a jewel may remain [in this world] through the power of his merits?
Having spoken thus, the two of them, having resolved to see the lord of the earth,
bowed to the Slayer of Jambha once the dance had ceased and departed for the mortal realm.
Having reached the capital of Purūravas in an instant,
the two entered unimpeded by the staff-bearers due to their divine majesty.
The two of them beheld him, who had applied the unguents for his bath,
appearing like the moon with its oily luster clinging to it as if from fresh butter or nectar.
His powerful body shone forth, adorned with the ornament of loveliness, its costly jeweled bracelets having been washed away after his bath.
The neck of that man, whose noose of ears was empty [of ornaments],
attained a particularly lovely appearance, even though it was devoid of the placement of any jewelry.
Having deliberated upon her boundaries of beauty and magnanimity, the two Aśvins praised her as the supreme marvel of the Creator’s craftsmanship.
With palms joined in reverence, he whose heart was pure asked those two— who had accepted seats out of affection— the reason for their arrival.
The two said: "O Lord of the Earth, we have come to behold your form, which is the ornament of the three worlds and the flower-bowed god of love himself."
Out of a natural regard for the unrestrained virtues of the creation of the world,
the creation of the Lord of Creatures was beheld as if it were the very essence of a curious spectacle.
You, the moon of the earth, have been beheld with your full orb;
what can be said of the joy obtained by drinking the nectar of your form?
Thus addressed with affection by the two of them, the king, his smile slightly blossoming,
spoke to them with great respect:
"By the very sight of you both, I have become a recipient of grace."
They come merely by virtue of their merit and demerit to be seen by those who wish to see them.
Attaining sacred fords, association with the virtuous, and the great festival of honoring those worthy of worship—
these constitute the collection of essences within this tasteless and insubstantial cycle of existence.
"Having bathed and anointed myself, I have not shown you the respectful worship appropriate for you, so that my merit might bear fruit and be free from the thorn of regret."
"Stay for a moment within the fire-sanctuary;
having performed my ablutions, I shall come to become the recipient of your worship and affection."
Thus addressed by him, the two went to the abode of the Fire-god out of curiosity, thinking, "We shall see the king bathed and adorned."
Then the king, having performed his ablutions and adorned with all his ornaments,
approached her presence accompanied by his domestic priest.
Seeing the protector of the earth adorned with a crown and shimmering pearl necklaces, the two of them,
dejected and with downcast faces, did not say anything at all for a moment.
When the king had completed his worship, the domestic priest asked them:
"Why does an appearance of displeasure seem to come over you two so suddenly?"
When questioned by the domestic priest, "Has our transgression of discipline perhaps become the cause [of this]?", the two of them spoke slowly to him.
It is not that we lack affection for you, nor is it a transgression on your part;
rather, it is the wonder at seeing all things being swallowed by time.
Just now this king was seen even while being anointed with oil in such a manner;
yet, through the ripening of time in an instant, he is no longer seen in that way at all.
While the forest of the fuel of days is constantly being consumed by the fire of the sun,
the variegated form is led by the smoke of time to its lack of variety.
Having ascertained that this impermanence is eternal for all phenomena,
who would maintain pride regarding form, which is like a painted canvas in a dream?
Having seen forms worn out by old age, bodies afflicted by disease, and lifespans devoured by time, who could possibly feel pride?
This world, which is observed to possess such vast forms and transformations,
consists of these very drops of semen that have reached a state of swelling.
Oh, how subtle is this progression of Time, its movement so imperceptible,
that through the ripening of its transformation, everything assumes an entirely different form!
That wave of beauty which belonged to the king’s body at the moment of his bath was drunk up by him in an instant, as he engaged in activities appropriate for another time.
For human beings, the measure of a full lifespan, as well as beauty and prosperity, flows away incessantly like water poured from a vessel during a journey.
As the divisions of time— kalās, kāṣṭhās, and muhūrtas— pass away with such speed,
they cannot be perceived individually, just as the movement of a lamp’s flames is not discernible.
The sun is made a child at dawn, a youth at midday, and an old man as it sets;
day after day, even the Lord of Day is subject to the play of time.
The oceans, embraced by the dense masses of their waves, dry up; the lords of mountains, towering with crowns of lofty peaks, go to ruin;
even the earth, together with the elephants of the quarters, falls away under whose power that all-consuming, ever-rushing, and somehow agitated Great Time (Mahākāla) perpetually hastens forth.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the king, the two Aśvins departed for heaven;
and the king, his pride stilled by the peace brought about by their words, became composed.
Therefore, having reflected, a wise person should not harbor pride in the playful charm of their wondrous beauty;
for in this dense expanse of worldly delusion, physical form is but a flash of lightning.
In the morning it is very young; then, by its budding state, it resembles the breasts of a beloved; thereafter, its beauty becomes lovely as it gradually unfolds with playful smiles;
then it reaches full bloom; afterwards, its body withers, becoming tremulous and limp; and on that very same day, scattered by the winds, the lotus dries up upon the bank, soaked and mired in mud.
In ancient times, Yayāti became disfigured by innate old age and lost his luster; Nala’s form became difficult to behold, his beauty having once surpassed the fame of Kāma.
Even the captivating body of Saudāsa became a source of terror to living beings. When beauty withers day by day and is impermanent, in what can one find steadfastness?
Therefore, having reflected upon the unstable nature of form, as well as the true nature of existence,
the wise should apply the appropriate remedy for the pacification of passion in order to attain the stable state.
The Fifth Reflection.

"I am a hero, skilled at shattering the ranks of cruel adversaries, a swift leader of the hosts of horses and elephants in the army"—thus does pride arise within men who have conquered the world with the strength of their own arms; yet when time has worn it away, that haughty arrogance becomes a cause for humiliation.
What kind of pride is this in a man’s heroism? Even among animals, a state of bravery is observed;
yet they do not call that "heroism" which is devoid of propriety, bereft of modesty, and impoverished of compassion.
The valor of a youth, who is like a flower, lies in striking his mother with a playful smile;
the valor of an old man, whose joints are slack, lies in praising himself on the paths of former tales.

In the third part of youth, that very valor which is overcome by the arising of pride undergoes a complete reversal in turn due to the manifold nature of the mind's fluctuations. (KDarp 5.4) ... [omitted] ...
What can be done for this mind, which is by nature as fickle as the wind and possesses diverse qualities? (KDarp 5.5)
He by whom the enemy armies were broken yesterday has become timid and unsteady today;

Śakra was swallowed by Vṛtra in battle, yet that same Śakra slew Vṛtra with foam. [The royal fortune] does not remain steady for one who is fickle with pride; like a drunken prostitute, she embraces only one man at a time.
That hero, the son of Jamadagni, who had severed the thousand arms of Kārtavīrya in battle,
became a supplicant for the sake of his Brahminhood when an arrow was placed upon the hand of Rāma.
Rāma, too, out of a desire to gain assistance, practiced the humility of seeking refuge with the monkey.

The majesty of a hero, when licked by Time as if by the winter season, attains a state of attenuation. (KDarp 5.9) The monkey Vālin, having forcibly seized with his hand the ten-faced Rāvaṇa—who was as capable as Mount Kailāsa of bearing the weight of joy—and having fixed him in the joint of the fold of his armpit, performed the ritual of twilight at the seven oceans. (KDarp 5.10)
The kings renowned for their martial prowess had previously been imprisoned by King Jarāsaṃdha;
yet he was split in two by Bhīmasena, whose weapon is his own arm, through the rending of that alliance.
Bhīma, too, his fortitude shattered by Karṇa and his power confounded, was spared out of mercy;
yet before Arjuna, whose bow was drawn, he fell from moment to moment into the state of a beggar.
Having abandoned the group of wives belonging to Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna departed, overcome by the force of the cowherds;
the course of valor, pursued by the path of destiny, is not known, being as fickle as the ear of an elephant.
The coward attains heroism, and even the hero falls into cowardice;
for this fickle valor, there is no constant stability anywhere.
Bāṇa, who had become a guest on the path of the edge of the discus of the enemy of Kaṃsa— the three-eyed Lord—
and who had been devoted from birth, was not protected despite being worthy of protection.
When Kālayavana was swiftly overcome, Śauri took refuge with Mucukunda,
his form curled up upon the surface of his bed.
When Śiśupāla’s head had been severed by the Discus-wielder with his discus,
the kings who were his partisans did not even cast their glances upon their bows.
The younger brother of Duryodhana was seen with his blood being violently drunk by Droṇa,
Karṇa, Kṛpa, and others— who were like women— though they were entirely weaponless.
With his two arms constricted by the expanded body of the python,
Vṛkodara became resonant with the sound of his mother’s piteous cries.
Even for the great men of old, such an abasement of pride occurred; by whom could this praise of their unrestrained and common valor not be welcomed?
Cruelty toward the weak, ferocity toward those who are powerful, steadfastness in the face of grave sins, deceitfulness in speech, and harshness— such is the "heroism" of the base.
The valor of one who is merciless without cause is called cruelty;
he who, like a serpent, is ever ready to strike at the lives of embodied beings.
This alone is the supreme valor: the protection of another's life;
for one who takes life is not a hero—a hero is he who bestows life upon those in need.
No quality whatsoever is produced by the valor of one devoid of intelligence;
provoked by the thundering of the clouds, the lion falls into a chasm.
What is the use of the prowess of an elephant intoxicated with rut and passion, who,
out of greed for the prize of a courtesan, casts his body into a pit?
What wonder is there in the valor of a servant who has sold his body, for whom death is certain like that of a sheep tied to the slaughter-block? (KDarp 5.26)
